outcome: Not settled as of 13 October 2026, and no event since 26 January 2024 proves or disproves infinitely many twin primes. What moved is the neighbouring bounded-gap constant H1 (the liminf of consecutive prime gaps), which went from 246 (Polymath8b, 2014) to a claimed 240 (Stadlmann, human, arXiv 31 Aug 2026), then to claimed bounds of 236 (Kintali, 1 Sep 2026, AI-assisted, system unnamed; Song and Yue ePrint 2026/1893, 4 Sep 2026), 212 (Axiom Math with AxiomProver, 3 Sep 2026) and 186 (OpenAI, attributed to GPT-6 Astra, 3 Sep 2026, Lean development conditional on three declared axioms). None of these is peer reviewed as far as I found, and none bounds gaps of size 2.
problem_asks: The statement asks one thing: that there are infinitely many twin primes, i.e. infinitely many primes p for which p+2 is also prime (equivalently, gap-2 pairs recur without end, which is liminf of consecutive prime gaps = 2). It does not ask for a bound on the gap, for other gap sizes, for an asymptotic count, or for any of the Hardy-Littlewood refinements. The statement is Wikipedia's January 2024 wording, which is Landau's second problem.

events.what_happened: J. R. Chen's theorem: infinitely many primes p such that p+2 is prime or a product of at most two primes. Dated from a search summary of the Wikipedia 'Twin prime' article; the section I fetched did not contain Chen, so this is not opened.
events.delivers: Infinitely many p with p+2 prime or semiprime. A partial result on the twin prime question, weaker than the bullet's infinitude of twin primes.
events.remains: Whether p+2 is prime infinitely often (the bullet's full claim).
events.direction: Partial result toward the conjecture; does not decide it.

events.what_happened: Yitang Zhang's announcement of a finite bound: infinitely many pairs of primes differing by at most N < 7 x 10^7 (Wikipedia gives the announcement as 17 April 2013; the Annals of Mathematics paper followed in 2014). Background, pre-window.
events.delivers: H1 < 7 x 10^7. Bounded gaps only; does not reach gap 2.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published Zhang's paper (2014 per the Wikipedia reference list)

events.direction: Bounded-gap result; does not decide gap 2.

events.what_happened: James Maynard's 'Small gaps between primes' (arXiv 1311.4600, posted November 2013 per the arXiv id), with H1 <= 600 and bounded-length results for m primes. Tao independently reached the same method, per Wikipedia. Background, pre-window. Not opened in this run; the arXiv id is cited from the Axiom project page.
events.delivers: H1 <= 600 unconditionally; the method gives bounds for m primes in bounded intervals. Bounded gaps only.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published Maynard's paper (2015 per the Wikipedia reference list)

events.direction: Bounded-gap result; does not decide gap 2.

events.what_happened: Polymath8b collaboration: H1 <= 246 by optimising Maynard's sieve and Zhang-type inputs using only Bombieri-Vinogradov (arXiv 1407.4897, posted July 2014 per the arXiv id; published in Research in the Mathematical Sciences). Background, pre-window. The 246 figure is still the value on the Wikipedia article's lead as fetched, and the Wikipedia 'Twin prime' page was last edited 4 Oct 2026 and still gives 246.
events.delivers: H1 <= 246. Bounded gaps only.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the Polymath8 paper (2014 per the Wikipedia reference list)

events.direction: Bounded-gap result; does not decide gap 2.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'A proof of the twin prime conjecture', arXiv 1707.03265 (math.GM). The abstract claims a lower bound (1+o(1)) x/(2C log^2 x) on the number of twin pairs up to x, with C a fixed constant, and concludes the count is infinite; it describes a general method for correlations sum G(n)G(n+l). Revised in 2021, 2022 and March 2026 (v4, 8 Mar 2026, 'reformatted, introduction expanded, ideas unchanged'). Dated to v1, the first public argument.
events.revisions: v1 26 Jun 2017; v2 28 Jul 2021; v3 4 Mar 2022; v4 8 Mar 2026 (current). No withdrawal notice shown on the abstract page.
events.delivers: Claims unconditional infinitude of twin primes (the full bullet), by a method claimed to estimate correlations sum G(n)G(n+l).
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim held; whether it holds is unestablished.
events.time_since_posted: about 9 years since v1; v4 revised March 2026 with no uptake I found
events.doubts: Claims a complete proof of a problem that has resisted for over a century, in math.GM; no journal acceptance or expert comment found in my searches. I read the abstract page only, not the 11-page text, so I have not checked the key estimate. The 2026 revision reportedly concedes that a complete proof remained elusive, per a search snippet that I did not open; not verified.
events.direction: Claims to prove the conjecture (asserts the bullet's claim).

events.what_happened: Berndt Gensel, 'On the Infinitude of the Twin Primes', arXiv 1909.07975. Proposes a reformulation via twin prime generators x with 6x-1 and 6x+1 both prime, using admissible residue classes and an adapted Selberg sieve. The abstract says that because of the parity problem a Selberg sieve alone cannot solve the problem. Latest revisions were in August 2025 (v5-v7).
events.revisions: v1 17 Sep 2019; v2 27 Jan 2020; v3 4 Feb 2020; v4 22 Mar 2020; v5 5 Aug 2025; v6 12 Aug 2025; v7 18 Aug 2025. No withdrawal shown.
events.delivers: A reformulation and an approach; no proof claimed in the abstract.
events.doubts: Abstract concedes the parity obstruction blocks the method it uses. Not a proof claim; recorded as discarded.
events.direction: Reformulation; does not claim to prove the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Frank Vega, 'The Smallest Gap Between Primes' (EasyChair/Qeios, May-June 2023, several versions) claims an arithmetic proof that the twin prime conjecture is true. From search snippets only; the EasyChair page I tried returned 404.
events.delivers: Claims the full conjecture.
events.doubts: Self-published on EasyChair/Qeios (open-review preprint servers, not refereed journals). Not opened; content unverified.

events.what_happened: 'The Infinitude of Twin Primes', International Journal of Mathematical, Digital and Engineering Sciences (ijmdes), article 282, published October 2025 per a search snippet. The snippet describes sorting twin primes by final digit to prove infinitude. Not opened; a second search did not surface the article.
events.delivers: Claims infinitude of twin primes (the full bullet), per snippet.
events.doubts: Small venue; I could not confirm acceptance details or any verification. Not opened.

events.what_happened: Zenodo record (two versions, September 2025, per a search snippet) claiming an unconditional proof by 'rail exclusion' modular arguments with explicit constants. Not opened.
events.delivers: Claims infinitude of twin primes, per snippet.
events.doubts: Self-published Zenodo record; no acceptance or expert comment found. Not opened.

events.what_happened: 'TWINION: Symbolic Recurrence of Irreducible Prime Pairs' on Cambridge Open Engage (May 2025, per snippet), using a symbolic framework called AION to claim a structural proof. Listing says not peer-reviewed. Not opened.
events.delivers: Claims infinitude of twin primes, per snippet.
events.doubts: Listing states not peer-reviewed. Not opened.

events.what_happened: Two Cambridge Open Engage working papers by an author named Gumpert, 'Proof of the infinity of twin primes', versions January and February 2025 (per a search snippet). The snippet gives only a one-line abstract. Not opened.
events.delivers: Claims infinitude of twin primes, per snippet.
events.doubts: Listing says not peer-reviewed. Not opened.

events.what_happened: Frank Vega, 'Note for the Small Gaps' (EasyChair, May 2024, per a search snippet). Argues by contradiction that the conjecture holds, while stating that there is no verified solution yet. The EasyChair page returned 404 on fetch; content from snippet only.
events.delivers: Claims the full conjecture by contradiction, per snippet.
events.doubts: Self-published EasyChair preprint; the author's own text is said to concede no verified solution exists. Not opened.

events.what_happened: Srikanth Cherukupally, 'An Equivalent form of Twin Prime Conjecture connected with a sequence of arithmetic progressions', arXiv 2603.08099 (math.NT). Gives an equivalent form via a symmetric property in a family of arithmetic progressions indexed by coprime pairs (a0, d0), with a reformulation in terms of |S(d0)| = 2 per a search snippet.
events.delivers: A reformulation of the conjecture. Does not claim proof.
events.remains: The bullet's claim, in equivalent form.
events.doubts: Only the abstract was read; the S(d0) equivalence and its proof were not checked. Recorded as a discarded reformulation.
events.direction: Reformulation; neither proves nor refutes the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Zenodo record published 13 March 2026 (v1, per a search snippet) presenting a 'complete-proof architecture' built on a chain of named theorems. Whether this is the record that the snippet describes was not confirmed; not opened.
events.delivers: Claims infinitude of twin primes, per snippet.
events.doubts: Self-published repository record. The search found no independent verification. Not opened.

events.what_happened: John R. Woodward and Alia Asheralieva (Heriot-Watt University), 'The Proof of the Twin-Prime Conjecture', a working paper on the Heriot-Watt research portal dated 6 April 2026. The abstract says the conjecture 'is still unsolved' and proposes 'a novel approach to theoretically validate the twin prime conjecture'.
events.delivers: Proposes an approach; the abstract does not claim a proof. Despite the title, it presents the conjecture as open.
events.doubts: Only the portal abstract was read; the approach is not described there, so I could not assess it. Recorded as discarded because it does not claim proof.
events.direction: Approach only; the abstract does not claim the conjecture is proved.

events.what_happened: Taha Muhammad, 'Twin Prime Conjecture (American Way)', Cambridge Open Engage working paper (DOI 10.33774/coe-2026-h89q0), posted 28 June 2026. Claims a proof by an inductive method extending a known twin pair to a larger one, using 'Taha's Detector Prime Number', a factorial-based primality criterion, and assuming a primality test exists for every integer.
events.delivers: Claims infinitude of twin primes (the full bullet) by induction.
events.remains: Nothing, if the induction held; the page states it has not been peer-reviewed.
events.doubts: Reader comment by 'Peter M' (28 June 2026) says the inductive step assumes a new pair of primes always yields a twin prime pair without showing it, and asks what happens if p2 is prime but q2 is not. The comment calls it 'not even remotely close to a proof'. The commenter's standing is not established. The paper's own assumption (a primality test for every integer) is a second visible gap.

events.what_happened: Two Cambridge Engage postings titled 'Twin Primes... (Revolution Way)' in July 2026 (per a search snippet) propose a structural approach based on linear forms. Not opened.
events.delivers: Claims a proof approach, per snippet.
events.doubts: Listed as not peer-reviewed. Not opened.

events.what_happened: Axiom Math released a machine-checked Lean 4 formalization of the 'BGP246 theorem' (infinitely many prime pairs differ by at most 246), together with the open PrimeGapsLib library. Axiom's project page dates the release to 17 August 2026; Axiom's X posts are dated 18 August. The human-written blueprint came first; AxiomProver then produced the Lean proofs. The result is a formalisation of Maynard (2013) and Polymath8b (2014), not new mathematics.
events.revisions: Repository has 7 commits as fetched; no dated version history read.
events.delivers: Formal proof that H1 <= 246, conditional in the README's words on the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem as the only named input (result 3 also uses an unspecified 'existence of certificate'). Bounded gaps only.
events.remains: Gap 2 is untouched. The formalisation does not reach H1 = 2.

checked_by.who: Lean Eval leaderboard entry 'zhang_bounded_prime_gaps' and a third-party Lean Eval submission
checked_by.qualification: Automated checking infrastructure and third-party builders
checked_by.what_they_did: The leaderboard entry for the 246 statement shows both 'declaration uses sorry' and 'All goals completed'; a third-party submission reportedly reuses PrimeGapsLib

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 with Mathlib and an internal fork of PrimeNumberTheoremAnd (per README)
machine_checked.sorry_free: Not confirmed by me. The README says the Comparator challenge file contains statement 1 of the Main Results 'with sorry as proof'; the repo's own review status is described as self-assessed (search snippet, not verified in the repo).

events.directly_checkable: Comparator challenge files in the repository (Comparator/comparator_fast.json; the README says the fast check takes minutes and the full one takes hours on Linux).
events.doubts: No independent human verification found. Axiom's own page frames the result ('the threshold of human knowledge', quoted via search by Ken Ono) in promotional terms. The formal statement must match the intended theorem, and the Comparator setup is the only independent check the repo offers. Nothing suggests the mathematics is wrong.
events.direction: Formal confirmation of an upper bound on H1; does not bear on whether gap 2 recurs.
people: Axiom Math team (41 named contributors on the project page; names not extracted)
Ken Ono (founding mathematician, per Axiom's framing)

events.what_happened: Julia Stadlmann, 'Bounded gaps between primes', arXiv 2608.31126 (v1 submitted 31 Aug 2026, single version as fetched). Combines the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem with newer equidistribution estimates for smooth moduli (Zhang-type, Polymath8a/8b framework) to get H1 <= 240, improving 246. The abstract states this and nothing about AI. Science News reports she is at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and was mentored by Kevin Ford. Science News also gives a 'by early summer 2026' timing that conflicts with its own August timeline.
events.delivers: H1 <= 240: infinitely many prime gaps of size at most 240. Bounded gaps only.
events.remains: Gap 2 (H1 = 2). The result does not reach it.

checked_by.who: Thomas Bloom (number theorist; qualification not checked in this run)
checked_by.what_they_did: Praised the result on X ('A great new result on gaps between primes (by a human!)'). Snippet only; the post was not opened and does not say the proof was checked.
Called the problem 'fiendishly difficult' and praised the work, as quoted in Science News. No statement of checking the proof.

events.doubts: No specific error identified. One Hacker News commenter says '240 was not a tight bound from her methods' and that she 'rushed to release her work' before an AI result; this is speculation, not analysis. Later claims (212, 186) build on her equidistribution estimates; any error there would propagate, but I found no such error reported. An Axiom paper, read only through a search summary, says her results depend on delicate numerics; not verified.
events.direction: Upper bound on H1 (bounded gaps); cuts toward nothing about gap 2.

events.what_happened: Shiva Kintali announced H1 <= 236 on X and on his personal homepage on 1 Sep 2026. The homepage gives it as 'Improved Bounded Gaps Between Primes. H1 <= 236' with a PDF at papers/Prime-Gaps.pdf (not opened). The homepage annotation quotes the author: 'Building upon Julia Stadlmann's ideas, I proved H1 <= 236 using AI.' The method is described as the GPY approach with the Maynard-Tao sieve. No model is named.
events.delivers: Claims H1 <= 236. Bounded gaps only.
events.doubts: VibeMathed records 'no preprint, no named model and no argument in public' as of its last check; the homepage does link a PDF, which I did not open, so the two sources disagree. VibeMathed grades it Candidate, Unreviewed. The author's own X post is cited only through a search snippet. Not refereed. A later claim (212) superseded it within two days.
events.direction: Upper bound on H1 (bounded gaps); cuts toward nothing about gap 2.

events.what_happened: Zhao Song and Song Yue (Northeastern University), 'Bounded Gaps Between Primes: An Upper Bound of 236', IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive 2026/1893, category Foundations. Received 4 Sep 2026, approved 9 Sep 2026 (the page shows no separate posting date). Claims H1 <= 236 and cites Stadlmann's 240 as the prior best. The page has no statement about methods, AI or acknowledgements.
events.delivers: Claims H1 <= 236. Bounded gaps only.
events.doubts: Posted in the Cryptology ePrint 'Foundations' category, an unusual home for a number theory result. Only the abstract page was read, not the PDF. Whether this is the same mathematics as the Kintali announcement, which also says 236, is not established.
events.direction: Upper bound on H1; cuts toward nothing about gap 2.

events.what_happened: OpenAI preprint 'Improved Short Gaps Between Primes' (cdn.openai.com PDF; header dated 30 Aug 2026 per secondary sources; public release 3 Sep 2026 with the GPT-6 Astra launch). Claims liminf (p_{n+1} - p_n) <= 186 by establishing DHL[40,2] from an admissible 40-tuple of diameter 186, combining the Polymath8a and Stadlmann equidistribution estimates with factorisation conditions on moduli that make certain divisor products densely divisible, which allows a larger Selberg support. Companion 'abridged chain of thought' document says exact finite searches give H(40) = 186 and H(41) = 188. Lean 4 development openai/PrimeGaps186 is conditional on three declared axioms (see machine_checked) plus a Python/FLINT numerical certificate. Not on arXiv, per search. Weijie Su's X post: 'Announcing that GPT-6 Astra has pushed the prime gap to 186, with Lean formalization!'. The post refers to 'our model', which suggests OpenAI staff, not confirmed.
events.revisions: Paper header 30 Aug 2026; public 3 Sep 2026. Tao's optimisation-constants repo merged a row for 186 on 5 Sep 2026 (PR #166, opened 4 Sep, branch deleted 26 Sep).
events.delivers: liminf (p_{n+1} - p_n) <= 186: infinitely many consecutive prime gaps of size at most 186, conditional on the three axioms in the Lean development (Kloosterman bound <= 3 attributed to Deligne/Katz; rank-two Kloosterman correlation bound attributed to Fouvry-Kowalski-Michel; 104 outer and 45 inner physical-integral bounds plus three cap bounds, numerically certified). Bounded gaps only.
events.remains: Gap 2. The paper's Theorem 1.1 concerns H1; it does not reach H1 = 2.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (README pins Lean 4.34.0-rc2); the registry issue reports kernel, Comparator and Nanoda checking
machine_checked.sorry_free: Not stated as sorry-free. The README says the registered build passed without errors or warnings, that the six permitted axioms include the three project axioms, and that Challenge.lean contains 'three intentional theorem placeholders'.

events.directly_checkable: The numerical certificate is run by python3 -B prime_gap_186_certificate.py --workers 4 --output <new path> (README). Its receipt says 'passed: true' but 'does not discharge any Lean axiom'.
events.doubts: The Lean result is conditional on three project axioms, which the README calls 'unproved inputs in this Lean development'. The formal proof is roughly 10 MB; a Hacker News commenter says it has had little review, and formalization.yaml says 'No independent human semantic review' and that a complete auxiliary-declaration audit is not established. The numerical integral and cap bounds are checked only by a Python/FLINT certificate. The registry grades the result 'Claimed', 'Provisional', 'Peer reviewed: No', and recommends 'under_verification' or 'partially_verified'. A search summary says Tao's record lists the 186 row with the same caveat; the commit behind that could not be fully verified (see incomplete).
events.direction: Upper bound on H1 (bounded gaps); cuts toward nothing about gap 2. It is the strongest bound claimed in the window.
events.object: An admissible 40-tuple of diameter 186 (the README calls it 'the included tuple of diameter 186'). It is a finite combinatorial certificate used to derive DHL[40,2]; it is not a counterexample to anything. Checked by the Lean development together with the numerical certificate.
people: Weijie Su (X announcement; affiliation not confirmed)

Swaminathan, Jesse Thorner, Yunzhou Xie) announced H1 <= 212 on 3 Sep 2026, 'building on Julia Stadlmann's work and extensive experiments on a massive distributed cluster' (Axiom post quoted by an aggregator). A preliminary draft is at primegaps.axiommath.ai/bgp212.pdf, which I could not read (the fetch returned binary). Axiom says a final version and Lean formalization will go to arXiv; none found yet.

events.delivers: Claims H1 <= 212. Bounded gaps only.

machine_checked.system: AxiomProver Lean certificate of the deduction (system version not stated in what I read)

events.doubts: Registry grades it 'Claimed'; 'Nobody outside the lab has checked this yet'. The Lean certificate covers only the deduction from stated inputs (Bombieri-Vinogradov and equidistribution estimates, per the registry), not the analytic inputs. The draft itself was not readable by me, so I cannot check its argument or whether the numerics are delicate. Sources disagree on who held 212 and when OpenAI's 186 followed (see disputes).
events.direction: Upper bound on H1; cuts toward nothing about gap 2.

events.what_happened: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra launch week also included a 'long gaps' PDF (cdn.openai.com/.../long_gaps.pdf) on large prime gaps. Per a tracker entry (not opened), Astra improved a term in a bound on large gaps unchanged for over 80 years. The PDF itself was not opened.

events.doubts: Not opened. Recorded so the later pass can see it is a different question (maximal gaps, not the minimal gap 2).

disputes.summary: Who held the sub-212 record, and in what order. Science News (opened) says Axiom's 212 came first and OpenAI's 186 followed within two hours; a Hacker News commenter says the same. A search summary of a LessWrong post (not opened) reportedly calls 212 an OpenAI figure. Not resolved.

Kintali (announced 236 with AI on 1 Sep 2026) and Song and Yue (ePrint 2026/1893, claims 236, received 4 Sep 2026) both claim H1 <= 236. Whether they are the same work is not established; the ePrint authors are different people.

Stadlmann's 240 is described by Science News as a human result and by an aggregator annotation as 'without using AI'. The arXiv abstract page itself names no AI tool. The downstream claims (212, 186) build on her estimates; Axiom's and OpenAI's papers credit her as independent concurrent work or as the source of the ideas, depending on the source.

Science News says OpenAI's 186 'came within two hours' of Axiom and that 'both records were surpassed by OpenAI'. Its own timeline is internally inconsistent: it says Stadlmann's result came 'by early summer 2026' but also that she posted on the last day of August.

summary: The problem is open. I ran 48 web searches and opened 23 sources (listed below with opened flags; the rest were read from snippets only). Within the window the only activity is on the neighbouring bounded-gap constant H1, which is not the gap-2 question the bullet asks. Stadlmann's human result (arXiv 2608.31126, 31 Aug 2026) gives H1 <= 240 with no AI named. Kintali's H1 <= 236 (1 Sep 2026) says it was done 'with the help of AI' and names no system. Song and Yue's ePrint 2026/1893 also claims 236 and names no AI. Axiom Math's H1 <= 212 (3 Sep 2026) rests on a draft that I could not read; the registry I did read says 'the mathematics is theirs' and AxiomProver generated the Lean certificate of the deduction. OpenAI's H1 <= 186 (paper dated 30 Aug, public 3 Sep 2026) is the strongest claim: its paper, as quoted by secondary sources, says 'the proof is due to GPT 6 Astra', and the Lean development is conditional on three declared axioms (two Kloosterman-type estimates attributed to Deligne/Katz and Fouvry-Kowalski-Michel, plus numerical integral and cap bounds checked by a Python/FLINT certificate). None of the post-2024 bounded-gap claims is peer reviewed, and the registries grade them 'Claimed' or 'Unreviewed'. Axiom's 246 formalisation (17-18 Aug 2026) formalises an existing result and is recorded but is not new mathematics. Many unrefereed twin-prime proof claims appeared on arXiv, Zenodo, EasyChair, Cambridge Open Engage and a small journal. I opened the arXiv pages of the two oldest and most-cited (Agama 2017, Gensel 2019), the 2026 Cambridge and Heriot-Watt postings, and the Cherukupally reformulation. None of them is accepted, and the Taha reader comment identifies a specific gap in the induction. No claim in the window addresses gap 2. Wikipedia's 'Twin prime' lead, last edited 4 Oct 2026, still gives 246 and mentions no 2026 result. Metaculus snapshots (not opened) put the median in the 2040s, not 2039. Close calls: (a) Whether bounded-gap constants count as 'a quantity the problem names'. The bullet names only infinitude of p+2 prime; H1 is linked but distinct, so the bounded-gap results touch a neighbouring quantity, and a careful reader could treat them as progress on the bullet or as a different question. (b) Whether AI was load-bearing in the Axiom 212 result. The registry says the mathematics is the authors' and AxiomProver made the Lean certificate; the draft could not be read, so I have not confirmed this. I have put AxiomProver in the event's note but not in ai.systems, because the stated role is formalisation of an argument the humans gave. (c) Whether the OpenAI 186 credit to GPT-6 Astra is load-bearing: the authors credit the proof itself, so I have listed it in ai.systems, but the quote is secondhand because the PDF was unreadable to me. Public mathematicians (Thomas Bloom, Kannan Soundararajan, Kevin Ford as mentor, Terence Tao critical of AI-first approaches) praised or commented on Stadlmann's work, but none is recorded as having verified an argument. Tao's own comments on the 186 result that I could find are about benchmarks, not correctness.
competing_reading: For the bullet: none of these results changes what a careful person would write about twin primes. The strongest reading that they do matter is that H1 is the quantity the twin prime conjecture is about (the conjecture is H1 = 2), so each new bound narrows the gap the conjecture must close; the Wikipedia article still names only the infinitude claim. For AI: the strongest reading that AI was load-bearing is the OpenAI paper's own attribution ('the proof is due to GPT 6 Astra') plus Su's 'GPT-6 finding complementary factorization conditions'; the strongest reading that it was not is that the Lean conditions are unproven inputs and the registries grade the result Claimed. For Axiom 212, the strongest case that AI was load-bearing is that AxiomProver generated the Lean certificate and the draft mentions 'extensive experiments on a massive distributed cluster'; the case against is the registry statement 'the mathematics is theirs'.
what_would_settle_it: For the bullet: a proof that infinitely many p have p+2 prime, or any argument that H1 = 2, refereed or checked by named experts. For the bounded-gap claims: the full text of Stadlmann's (already readable), Kintali's PDF, Song and Yue's PDF, Axiom's bgp212.pdf and any arXiv version, and OpenAI's paper PDF as read directly, plus a human referee report or journal acceptance, or an independent reproduction of the Lean development with its three axioms. For AI attribution: the exact sentences in the OpenAI PDF and Axiom draft about who produced the key idea and the numerics, and a statement from Axiom or Kintali naming the system used.

event.what_happened: Julia Stadlmann, 'Bounded gaps between primes', arXiv 2608.31126 (v1 submitted 31 Aug 2026, single version as fetched). Combines the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem with newer equidistribution estimates for smooth moduli (Zhang-type, Polymath8a/8b framework) to get H1 <= 240, improving 246. The abstract states this and nothing about AI. Science News reports she is at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and was mentored by Kevin Ford. Science News also gives a 'by early summer 2026' timing that conflicts with its own August timeline.
event.delivers: H1 <= 240: infinitely many prime gaps of size at most 240. Bounded gaps only.
event.remains: Gap 2 (H1 = 2). The result does not reach it.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether there are infinitely many twin primes, which is equivalent to liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n) = 2. I read the bounded-gap constant H1 as the quantity whose value the conjecture fixes, so the improvements to H1 (Zhang, Maynard, Polymath8b, Stadlmann 240, Kintali and Song-Yue 236, Axiom 212, OpenAI 186) are answered `bound` rather than `variant`. Chen's 'prime or semiprime' theorem changes the question itself, so it is `variant`. The long-gaps paper is about a different quantity (maximal gaps), so it is also `variant`. The Axiom 246 Lean release formalises known results, which makes it `none`. Every amateur claim of a full proof has the F10 signals together: a landmark claim, no uptake, the field still calling the problem open, and self-publishing or marginal venues. Those are `not_credible`. Taha's is `knocked_down` because of a specific gap in the induction that nobody has answered. On AI: OpenAI 186 is `generated`, on the paper's own (secondhand) attribution of the proof to GPT-6 Astra. Kintali and Axiom 212 list no systems credited with mathematics, so both are `none`; AxiomProver produced only the Lean certificate.
judgement.doubts: Close call: someone could argue that bounds on H1 are a variant question and not a bound on the twin prime statement. I chose `bound` because the conjecture is exactly H1 = 2. The GPT-6 Astra attribution is quoted from secondary sources because the PDF was unreadable. Kintali's 'I proved H1 <= 236 using AI' was not placed in ai.systems, so I answered `none`; if that is treated as a credit, it would be at most `assisted` with no model named. The Lean development behind the 186 result is conditional on three axioms, and its numerics are certified only by Python.
